paragraphs: The amount of dogmatic belief varies from one period to another. It arises in different ways, and it may change its object or its form. But dogmatic belief will never cease to exist under any circumstances. In other words, people will never stop holding some opinions on trust, without testing them by actual discussion. If everyone set out to form his own opinions and to seek the truth by paths he had cut for himself alone, we could not suppose that any considerable number of people would ever come to share a common belief. Yet it is obvious that without such a common belief no society can prosper — or rather, no society can survive. For without ideas held in common there is no common action, and without common action there may still be individuals, but there is no social body. For a society to exist, and all the more for it to prosper, the minds of its citizens must be drawn together and held together by certain dominant ideas. That cannot happen unless each citizen sometimes draws his opinions from the common source and agrees to accept certain beliefs from the community.

If I now consider man as an individual, I find that dogmatic belief is just as indispensable to him for living alone as it is for cooperating with his fellow creatures. If a man had to prove to himself every truth he uses in daily life, his task would never end. He would exhaust his strength on preliminary exercises and never get beyond them. His life is too short for this, and his intelligence too limited. So he is reduced to taking on trust a number of facts and opinions that he has had neither the time nor the ability to verify himself, but which people of greater ability have worked out, or which the world has adopted. On this foundation he builds the structure of his own thoughts. He does not proceed this way so much by choice as because the inflexible law of his condition forces him to. No philosopher in the world is so gifted that he does not believe a million things on the word of other people, and assume many more truths than he proves. This is not only necessary but desirable. A man who undertook to investigate everything for himself could give each thing only a little time and attention. His task would keep his mind in constant turmoil, which would stop him from penetrating to the depths of any truth or fastening his mind firmly to any conviction. His intellect would be at once independent and powerless. He must therefore choose among the various objects of human belief, and he must adopt many opinions without discussion, so that he can examine more thoroughly the smaller number he sets aside for investigation. It is true that whoever accepts an opinion on another person’s word thereby puts his mind in bondage to that extent. But it is a salutary bondage, one that lets him make good use of his freedom.

A principle of authority must therefore always be present, whatever the circumstances, in some part of the moral and intellectual world. Its place may vary, but it necessarily has one. The independence of individual minds may be greater or smaller, but it can never be unlimited. So the question is not whether any intellectual authority exists in the ages of democracy. It is simply where that authority resides and by what standard it is to be measured.

I showed in the preceding chapter how the equality of conditions leads men to a kind of instinctive disbelief in the supernatural, and to a very high and often exaggerated opinion of the human understanding. People who live in a period of social equality are therefore not easily led to place the intellectual authority they bow to beyond or above humanity. They usually look for the sources of truth in themselves, or in those who are like themselves. This alone would be enough to prove that no new religion could be established in such periods, and that any scheme for founding one would be not only impious but absurd and irrational. We can foresee that a democratic people will not easily believe in divine missions, that they will readily make fun of modern prophets, and that they will look for the chief judge of their beliefs within the limits of mankind, not beyond them.

When the ranks of society are unequal and people differ in condition, some individuals hold all the power of superior intelligence, learning, and education, while the multitude is sunk in ignorance and prejudice. People who live in these aristocratic periods are therefore naturally led to shape their opinions by the higher standard of one person or one class, and they are reluctant to recognize the infallibility of the mass of the people.

The opposite happens in ages of equality. The closer citizens come to the common level of an equal and similar condition, the less inclined each of them is to place unquestioning faith in a particular man or a particular class. But his readiness to believe the multitude grows, and opinion becomes more than ever the mistress of the world. Among a democratic people, common opinion is not only the one guide that private judgment retains. It also has a power there far beyond what it has anywhere else. In times of equality, people have no faith in one another, because they all resemble one another. But this same resemblance gives them almost unlimited confidence in the judgment of the public. For they all have equal means of judging, so it hardly seems likely that the greater truth would fail to lie with the greater number.

When the inhabitant of a democratic country compares himself individually with all those around him, he feels with pride that he is the equal of any one of them. But when he surveys the whole body of his fellows and sets himself against so huge a mass, he is at once overwhelmed by the sense of his own insignificance and weakness. The same equality that makes him independent of each of his fellow citizens taken one by one leaves him alone and unprotected against the influence of the greater number. Among a democratic people, then, the public has a singular power, of which aristocratic nations could never even form an idea. For it does not persuade people to adopt certain opinions. It enforces them, and instills them into the faculties by a kind of enormous pressure of the minds of all upon the reason of each.

In the United States the majority undertakes to supply individuals with a multitude of ready-made opinions, and so relieves them of the need to form opinions of their own. Everyone there adopts great numbers of theories on philosophy, morals, and politics without inquiry, on public trust. And if we look very closely, we will see that religion herself holds sway there much less as a doctrine of revelation than as a commonly received opinion. The political laws of the Americans give the majority sovereign rule over the community, and this materially increases the power the majority naturally exercises over the mind. For nothing is more common in man than to recognize superior wisdom in the person of his oppressor. This political omnipotence of the majority in the United States undoubtedly increases the influence that public opinion would have over each member of the community even without it. But the foundations of that influence do not rest on it. They must be sought in the principle of equality itself, not in the more or less popular institutions that people living under that condition may give themselves. The intellectual dominion of the greater number would probably be less absolute among a democratic people governed by a king than in a pure democracy, but it will always be extremely absolute. And whatever political laws govern people in the ages of equality, we can foresee that faith in public opinion will become a kind of religion there, with the majority as its ministering prophet.

Intellectual authority will therefore be different, but it will not be diminished. Far from thinking that it will disappear, I predict that it may easily gain too much weight and confine the action of private judgment within narrower limits than are suited either to the greatness or to the happiness of the human race. In the principle of equality I see two tendencies very clearly. One leads the mind of every man toward untried thoughts. The other would forbid him to think at all. And I can see how, under certain laws, democracy would extinguish that liberty of the mind to which a democratic social condition is favorable. After breaking every bond once imposed on it by ranks or by individuals, the human mind would then be tightly bound to the general will of the greatest number.

Suppose democratic nations were to replace all the different powers that checked or slowed the energy of individual minds too much with the absolute power of the majority. The evil would only have changed its symptoms. People would not have found a way to live independently. They would simply have invented (and it is no easy task) a new dress for servitude. There is here — and I cannot repeat it too often — much for deep reflection by those who regard freedom as a holy thing, and who hate not only the despot but despotism. For my own part, when I feel the hand of power pressing heavily on my brow, I care little who is oppressing me. And I am no more willing to bow beneath the yoke because a million arms hold it out to me.
